title: Why would God let this happen?
seoTitle: Why Does God Allow Suffering? An Honest Christian Answer
description: When something terrible happens, the question isn't academic. What the Bible says, what Christianity doesn't claim, and where God is in it.
summary: For the graveside and the hard argument alike: what the Bible says when God doesn't explain, and why the question is allowed.
askedAs: why did God let this happen
why do bad things happen to good people
where is God when it hurts
if God is good why is there evil
What does the Bible say about suffering?
answer: If you're asking this, something has happened that shouldn't have, and the question is coming out of you more like a cry than a thought. You don't have to make sense of it tonight, or accept anyone's tidy reason for it. The Bible asks this question out loud, and Jesus asked it from the cross. Christianity doesn't promise you'll be shown why. It says God didn't keep a safe distance from suffering, that he entered it, and that he will end it. Tonight, say it to God in whatever words you have, and let one person sit with you who won't try to explain. If this has left you not wanting to live, call or text one of the lines just below now. If you're asking with a clearer head, as a skeptic or a believer who can't make it fit, the objection is serious, and nothing here will pretend otherwise.
happening:
There are two ways to ask this. One is asked at a graveside, in a hospital corridor, in the car outside the doctor's office, on the night the phone rang. It's less a request for information than a cry with a question mark at the end, and under it are harder questions: *Where were you? Could you have stopped this? Can I still trust you?* The other is asked with a clearer head, by a skeptic or a believer who has seen enough of the world to wonder how a good and powerful God fits with it. Both are honest. They need different things, and a lot of harm is done by answering one as if it were the other.

If you're asking the first way, you may be feeling several things at once: grief, anger at God, shame about being angry at God, and a sick sense that the ground under your faith has shifted. You may have prayed for exactly the thing that didn't happen. Some people hear a darker whisper, *this is what I get*, and wonder whether God is punishing them. And kind people may be handing you sentences that make it worse: *everything happens for a reason*, *God needed another angel*, *God won't give you more than you can handle*.

There is some truth in the usual explanations. A mind in shock hunts for causes, because a reason feels like control, and that hunt is part of how people absorb a blow. Grief and shock are also physical, and they can scramble sleep, appetite, and concentration for weeks. And Scripture does say that God can bring good out of evil.

What the explanations leave out is the person asking. They treat the question as a request for information, when it's usually a cry for someone. In the notebooks C. S. Lewis kept after his wife, Joy, died in 1960, later published as *A Grief Observed*, his worst fear isn't that God doesn't exist. It's that God might not be good. That is the graveside question. It's asked from inside a relationship, and the Bible answers it the way you answer a person: by coming close.

scripture.intro: The Bible doesn't hush people who ask this. It gives you a man who argued with God and was vindicated, poems written after a city burned, a Savior who asked *why* from the cross, an apostle who groaned with the whole creation, and a promise about the end. Read them slowly.

passages.text: After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has. ... Then My servant Job will pray for you, for I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken accurately about Me, as My servant Job has.”
passages.reading: Job loses his children, his wealth, and his health, and he is never told why; only the reader sees the scene in heaven in chapters 1 and 2. His friends sit with him in silence for a week (Job 2:13), and then they start explaining: God is just, so Job must have sinned. Job refuses, and he takes his protest straight to God, while the friends only ever talk about God. When the LORD finally speaks from the whirlwind, he gives no reason. He gives himself, and Job says, "now my eyes have seen You" (Job 42:5). Job is humbled. But it's the friends, with their tidy explanations, who stand under God's anger, and they need the man they lectured to pray for them.

passages.text: You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation. Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long? Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return; renew our days as of old, unless You have utterly rejected us and remain angry with us beyond measure.
passages.reading: Lamentations is five poems written after the Babylonians burned Jerusalem and its temple, and the poet doesn't look away; children faint in the streets (Lamentations 2:11). These are the book's last lines, and they hold together what we keep trying to pull apart. The poet confesses that God reigns forever and, in the next breath, asks him why he has forgotten them. He prays the tension instead of resolving it. There's hope in the middle of the book, the famous line about mercies new every morning (Lamentations 3:22-23), but the book doesn't end there. It ends on a request and a fear. The Bible kept a book that closes on an open question, and there's room in it for your prayers that don't resolve either.

passages.text: From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land. At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
passages.reading: Mark keeps the words in the Aramaic Jesus spoke, and they're a quotation: the first line of Psalm 22, a lament that bears David's name. Jesus prays a lament while he is dying in the dark. Here Christianity parts company with every theory about suffering. In Jesus, God came into the pain himself, all the way to an execution, and the prayer on his lips there was a question. Psalm 22 goes on to say that God "has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted" (Psalm 22:24), and the resurrection is not far off. But the Gospels don't hurry past Friday. If *why* is the only prayer you have left, you're praying the words Jesus prayed.

passages.text: We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time. Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies. ... In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. ... And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.
passages.reading: Romans 8:28 is often handed to grieving people like a bandage. In its place it reads differently. Paul, writing to believers in Rome, had been beaten, stoned, and shipwrecked (he lists it in 2 Corinthians 11), and here he says the whole creation groans like a woman in labor, that believers groan with it, and that when we can't find words to pray, the Spirit groans for us. Only then comes the promise. It says God works all things together for good; it doesn't say all things are good. The good is named in the next verse: being made like his Son. It's a promise to hold in the dark. The groaning is real, it's headed somewhere, and it will end.

passages.text: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God. ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.” And the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.”
passages.reading: Earlier in Revelation, the martyrs cry out, "How long, O Lord" (Revelation 6:10). This is the answer the book finally gives them, and what it offers is an ending rather than an explanation. John saw it while he was, in his own words, a "partner in the tribulation" (Revelation 1:9), writing to churches that included one facing poverty and prison (Revelation 2:9-10). God's presence comes first: he makes his dwelling with his people. Then he wipes away every tear himself and names what will be no more: death, mourning, crying, and pain. The one on the throne says he is making all things new. He isn't finished yet, and the book doesn't pretend he is.

whyHard:
Start with the objection at full strength, because it has earned that. An old dilemma, often credited to the Greek philosopher Epicurus, runs like this: if God wants to stop evil but can't, he isn't all-powerful; if he can but won't, he isn't good; if he both can and wants to, where does evil come from? In his *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*, published in 1779, David Hume put those old questions in the mouth of Philo, the skeptic, and then had him press a harder point. Suppose a good God and a suffering world don't strictly contradict each other; still, no one reasoning honestly from a world like this one would conclude that its maker is both perfectly good and all-powerful. That more modest claim, that the world we actually live in makes God unlikely rather than impossible, is harder to answer, and it has shaped the case against God ever since. A century later Dostoevsky gave the argument a face. In *The Brothers Karamazov*, finished in 1880, Ivan Karamazov tells his believing brother, Alyosha, story after story of cruelty to children, then refuses any final harmony bought with their suffering. Ivan says it isn't God he rejects, and he hands back his ticket anyway. His is a moral protest more than a logic puzzle, and I don't know a stronger form of the question.

I came to faith from atheism, and I'm the father of five sons. I won't pretend this objection is weak, and I won't answer Ivan with a diagram. Some of what he says is simply true. A world where children suffer is not the world as it should be, and any account of God that asks you to call that suffering good deserves to lose.

There are three ways out of the dilemma, and everyone standing in the wreckage feels the pull of one of them. The first is to decide there is no God. The second keeps God good and makes him smaller: he hates this, but he couldn't stop it. Rabbi Harold Kushner, whose son died at fourteen, gave that answer in *When Bad Things Happen to Good People* (1981), and no one should sneer at an answer found inside a wound like that. The third keeps God powerful by making the suffering smaller, as if it were not really evil: *it's a blessing in disguise*, *God is teaching you something*, or, harshest of all, *you must have deserved it*. That's the road Job's friends took, and it's still well traveled in churches.

Scripture refuses all three. The poet of Lamentations, praying over the ruins of Jerusalem, confesses that God reigns forever, and the same book insists, "He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men" (Lamentations 3:33). It keeps God's power and God's goodness without shrinking the suffering, and it holds them together in prayer rather than in a system. Why do we reach for the exits anyway? Job told his friends why: "you see terror, and you are afraid" (Job 6:21). The explanations were for them. If Job suffered because he sinned, they were safe as long as they didn't. Most of our tidy sentences at funerals work the same way. I have to include myself here, because pastors are professional explainers, and the pull to make a room feel safe again is strong. Some of us also preached a faith that couldn't survive a hospital: the prosperity promise that faith brings health and wealth, or the softer version in which God exists to make life go well. When that faith breaks at a graveside, people conclude that God failed, when what failed was a God the Bible never described.

Be clear, then, about what Christianity claims, because it is harder and better than any of the exits: evil is real and God hates it, in Jesus he went into it all the way to death, and he will end it. It doesn't say suffering is an illusion, or secretly good, or always a punishment, or something believers are spared, and it doesn't promise that every suffering has a reason you'll be shown in this life. I can't tell you why God permitted the thing that brought you here, and you should be wary of anyone who says they can. When Ivan finishes, Alyosha answers by pointing to the one innocent who gave his own blood for all, and so has the right to forgive. Why would God let this happen? Christianity can't hand you every reason. It can tell you that once, outside Jerusalem, God let it happen to himself.

thisWeek.intro: You don't have to settle this question this week. Start smaller: talk to God, let one person near you, and look after your body. Do the first step today, and let the rest wait until you can.

steps.title: Say it to God in the words you have
steps.body: Tell God what happened and what you think of it, anger included. Job did, and so did the psalmists. If you can't find words, borrow theirs. Psalm 13 begins, "How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). Read it aloud once a day this week and add one sentence of your own at the end, even if the sentence is only *I don't understand*.

steps.title: Ask one person to sit with you
steps.body: Choose one person who can be with you without explaining anything: a friend, a relative who knows how to be quiet, a pastor. Tell them plainly, *I don't need answers. I just don't want to be alone with this.* Most people are relieved to be told how to help.

steps.title: Keep your body going
steps.body: Your body is carrying this too. Eat something, even if it's small, drink water, keep regular times for sleep, and get outside for a short walk each day. None of this answers the question, but hunger and sleeplessness make every question darker. If days go by without real sleep or food, call your doctor.

steps.title: Set the explanations down for now
steps.body: You'll hear reasons from kind people, and you may be producing your own at three in the morning. You don't have to accept them or argue with them this week. When one comes, you can say, *I'm not ready to make sense of this*, and leave it there. If a sentence has lodged in you and hurts, write it down and take it to a pastor later. Refusing a bad explanation isn't refusing God.

steps.title: Read the end of Job and one lament
steps.body: Once this week, in a quiet half hour, read [Job 38 through 42](/study/bible/job/38) in one sitting. Watch for two things: God never tells Job why, and Job is the one God defends. Then read Lamentations 3 and see where the hope sits, in the middle of the grief rather than after it.

steps.title: If it's an argument, give it a serious hour
steps.body: Read the strongest statement of the objection you can find next to the strongest Christian response; the essays and studies below do both. Then write down which part of it grips you most: the sheer amount of suffering in the world, one particular case, or the silence of God. A question named precisely is a question you can begin to carry.

moreHelp.body:
Asking why God allowed something isn't a sign that anything is wrong with you. It's one of the oldest prayers there is. But some suffering needs more than a pastor can give. If what happened was sudden, violent, or traumatic, if you saw it happen, or if weeks have passed and you still can't sleep, work, or care for the people who depend on you, talk with a licensed counselor as well as your pastor. The same is true if your questions about God have hardened into a settled certainty that nothing will ever be good again.

To find someone, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor who knows which local counselors are good with grief and respectful of faith. If you want a Christian counselor, make sure they're licensed in your state; your state's licensing board website will show it. A licensed counselor who doesn't share your faith can still help a great deal.

If you're having thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now, or call 911 if you're in danger. Making that call is a faithful thing to do.
signs: You're having thoughts of ending your life, or of not wanting to wake up. Call or text 988 now.
What happened was violent or a crime, or someone is still hurting you. Call 911 if you're in danger, and ask about a victim advocate.
Weeks have passed and you still can't sleep, eat, work, or care for the people who depend on you.
You keep reliving what happened, with images or panic that won't let up.
You're using alcohol, pills, or other drugs to get through the day.
You're a teenager carrying this alone. Tell a parent, a school counselor, or another adult you trust.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't have to explain everything on the first call. You can say something as simple as *Something terrible happened, and I'm not coping well. I'd like to see someone who works with grief.* Ask whether they have openings, whether they take your insurance, and what they charge if they don't. If your faith matters to you, say so: *I'm a Christian, and right now I'm struggling with God. Are you comfortable with that?* A good counselor, Christian or not, will answer plainly.
moreHelp.cost: Costs vary widely, so ask. Many counselors offer sliding-scale fees based on income. Community mental health centers provide lower-cost care, and university training clinics often see clients at reduced rates with supervised counselors in training. If you have a job, see whether your employer has an employee assistance program; many include a few free sessions. Hospices and churches often run free grief groups, and many churches keep a benevolence fund that can help pay for counseling. Ask your pastor.

helping.body:
If someone you love is asking this, your first job is to stay, not to answer. Job's friends were at their best in the first week, when they sat on the ground with him and said nothing (Job 2:13), and at their worst when they started defending God. The urge to explain is usually about us; it makes the world feel safe again for the helper.

So let them be angry, including at God, without correcting them. You don't need to defend God; he rebuked the men who tried. Say less than you think you should and stay longer than you think you should. Bring food, run the errand, say the name of the person who died. Scripture's instruction is short: "weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15).

If you're a pastor, be careful with Romans 8:28 at a casket, and let the family hear the laments before they hear the promise. And if the person asking is a skeptic, or a believer whose faith is coming apart, don't treat the question as an attack. Read the strongest version of it with them. They'll trust your faith more if it can survive their question.
say: I don't know why this happened. I'm so sorry.
You don't have to make sense of this for me.
You can say anything to me, including what you're feeling about God.
I'm bringing dinner on Thursday. You don't have to talk.
I'll keep praying when you can't.
dontSay: God won't give you more than you can handle.
At least it was quick, or any other sentence that starts with at least.
Maybe God is trying to teach you something.
I know exactly how you feel.
helping.next: Write down the hard dates, the anniversary, birthdays, the first holidays, and reach out on them, because the calls usually thin out after the funeral. Keep inviting them to ordinary things, and don't take a no personally. If they talk about wanting to die or not being able to go on, ask them directly whether they're thinking of ending their life, stay with them, and help them call or text 988, or call 911 if they're in danger right now. And bring in a pastor or a counselor when it's more than you can carry.

prayer:
Lord, I don't understand what you've allowed, and I'm not going to pretend I do. You heard Job when he shouted. You heard the poet in the ashes of Jerusalem. You heard your own Son ask why. Hear me.

I'm angry, and I'm afraid, and some nights I'm not sure you're there. If you won't give me a reason, give me yourself. Sit with me in this. When I can't pray, let your Spirit pray for me with the groans I don't have words for.

Guard me from the easy lies, the ones that make you smaller and the ones that make this smaller. Keep me honest, and keep me close, even when I push you away.

You have promised to wipe away every tear. I'm holding you to that. Until then, hold on to me, because I can't always hold on to you.

In the name of Jesus, who knows this from the inside. Amen.

faq.a: Christians have given partial answers, and each holds some truth. God made creatures with real freedom, and freedom can be used for cruelty. The creation itself is broken, and Paul says it groans, waiting to be set free (Romans 8:21-22). God can bring good even out of evil, as Joseph told the brothers who sold him (Genesis 50:20). But none of these explains why this particular thing happened, and the Bible never promises you'll be shown that in this life. Job never was told. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes, who searched as hard as anyone, concluded that "even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend" (Ecclesiastes 8:17). What the Bible gives instead is a God who entered suffering in Jesus and has promised to end it. That is less than an explanation, and more than one.

Jesus met this question more than once, and each time he refused the equation. When people told him about Galileans whom Pilate had killed, he asked whether they were worse sinners than everyone else and answered, "No, I tell you" (Luke 13:3). He said the same of eighteen people crushed when a tower fell, and turned the call to repent on everyone listening. When his disciples asked whose sin had made a man blind from birth, he said, "Neither this man nor his parents sinned" (John 9:3). Scripture speaks of God's discipline, but it forbids reading a tragedy as proof of special guilt. If you have sin to confess, confess it and receive forgiveness. Don't let anyone, including the voice in your own head, tell you God did this to get even.

faq.q: Did God cause this, or did he just allow it?
faq.a: Faithful Christians answer this differently, and it helps to know that before anyone makes you choose. The Reformed tradition holds that God ordains whatever comes to pass, evil included, without being its author or approving it, so nothing that happens to you is random or outside a Father's hand. Its clearest case is the cross, which Scripture calls both God's set plan and the work of lawless hands (Acts 2:23): God's purpose in it was good, and the guilt belonged to the men who did it. The Arminian and Wesleyan traditions hold that God permits evil without ordaining it, as the cost of a world where love can be freely given, and grieves it, so you never have to believe God planned what happened to you. They point to the line that God "does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men" (Lamentations 3:33). Both hold what matters most: God is good, he is not the author of evil, and he will judge and end it. This question divides faithful churches, not the faith, and you can leave it open and still trust him.

faq.q: Is it wrong to be angry at God?
faq.a: Anger at God, brought to God, is one of the oldest kinds of prayer in the Bible. Job asked, "Why do You hide Your face and consider me as Your enemy?" (Job 13:24). God answered him sharply from the whirlwind, but in the end he said Job had spoken rightly about him while his friends, for all their piety, had not (Job 42:7). A psalm asks, "Why, O LORD, do You stand far off?" (Psalm 10:1). What Scripture warns against is turning away from God, or turning the anger on other people. So say it to him. The God who answered Job from the whirlwind is not too fragile to hear it.

faq.q: If God is good, why doesn't he stop it?
faq.a: The Bible's answer is that he will, and that the delay isn't indifference. Answering scoffers who say Jesus's promised return is never coming, the second letter of Peter says, "The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish" (2 Peter 3:9). That's hard to hear from inside suffering, and it doesn't settle every case. But it names something true. If God ended all evil tonight, he would have to decide where evil stops, and it doesn't stop at other people; it runs through every one of us. Until that day, Christians are allowed to keep asking him, as the martyrs in Revelation do, how long.

slots.note: James came to faith from atheism. If the problem of evil figured in his unbelief or in his coming to faith, a paragraph in his own words on how he held the objection then and how he holds it now would give this section its full weight. The page claims only that he came to faith from atheism and will not pretend the objection is weak.

James was raised without a father and is raising five sons. If he wants, a sentence in his own words on how a child reads a father's absence or silence, or on what fatherhood has taught him about a love that does not explain itself, would deepen the Ivan passage. The page says only that he is the father of five sons.
A moment from James's ministry, in his own words and with details changed or permission given, when he chose to sit with a grieving person rather than explain. Nothing of the kind is claimed now.

Where James lands on whether God ordains or permits evil. The FAQ states the Reformed and the Arminian and Wesleyan accounts without a landing, as the contested-doctrine rule requires; he may add his own position and the tradition it comes from, in his own words.

sources.claim: A statement of the problem of evil attributed to Epicurus was cited by David Hume in his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779).
Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion was published in 1779, after his death in 1776.
sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion

sources.claim: In Part X of the Dialogues, Philo says that Epicurus's old questions are yet unanswered.
sources.cite: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Part X (Wikisource)

sources.claim: In Part XI of the Dialogues, Philo grants for argument's sake that misery is compatible with a God of infinite power and goodness, but argues that such a God cannot be inferred from the mixed good and ill of this world.
sources.cite: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Part XI (Wikisource)

sources.claim: Modern evidential arguments from evil, which hold that the good and evil we know make theism improbable rather than impossible, descend from Philo's argument in Hume's Dialogues.
sources.cite: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Humean Arguments from Evil against Theism (Timothy Perrine)

sources.claim: The Brothers Karamazov was first published serially in 1879 to 1880 and finished in 1880; in the chapter Rebellion, Ivan indicts God for a world in which children suffer.
sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Fyodor Dostoyevsky: The Brothers Karamazov

sources.claim: Ivan says it is not God he rejects and returns his ticket; Alyosha answers that there is a Being who can forgive everything because he gave his innocent blood for all.
sources.cite: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book V, chapter 4, Rebellion, Constance Garnett translation (Wikisource)

sources.claim: Joy Davidman died on July 13, 1960; the journals Lewis kept afterward were published in 1961 as A Grief Observed.
sources.cite: C.S. Lewis Institute, A Grief Observed

sources.claim: In A Grief Observed Lewis writes that his real danger was not ceasing to believe in God but coming to believe dreadful things about him.
sources.cite: C.S. Lewis Institute, C.S. Lewis on Grief

sources.claim: Harold Kushner's When Bad Things Happen to Good People (1981) followed the death of his son Aaron, of progeria, just after his fourteenth birthday, and proposed a God who hates suffering but cannot eliminate it.
sources.cite: Jewish Telegraphic Agency, obituary of Rabbi Harold Kushner, April 28, 2023

Outside claims were re-checked through search-engine excerpts of the named sources (direct fetches are still blocked from this environment; re-open each before release): Hume's Dialogues published in 1779, with Epicurus's questions in Part X and Philo's inference argument in Part XI; The Brothers Karamazov serialized 1879 to 1880 and finished in 1880; Ivan's returned ticket and Alyosha's reply; Lewis's fear in A Grief Observed that God might not be good; Kushner's son Aaron, dead at fourteen, and the 1981 book. Job's friends were re-checked against the BSB: they address only Job, never God. Changes: sensitivity raised to high with crisisTopics suicide, since the signs name thoughts of ending your life, and the answer now points to the lines below. The steelman now includes Philo's harder, evidential argument, the form the objection's defenders press (sourced to Part XI and the IEP). Corrected: Alyosha answers by pointing to the Being who gave his innocent blood, not with a name; Ivan's words paraphrased exactly; the novel 'finished in 1880'; the third exit now names calling suffering something other than evil, so it no longer sweeps in serious theodicies; Lamentations no longer placed in Jerusalem; Psalm 22 said to bear David's name; Revelation 2:9-10 no longer generalized to all the churches; 2 Peter cited as the second letter of Peter, answering scoffers as the letter frames them. FAQ: Deuteronomy 29:29 replaced by Job and Ecclesiastes 8:17, because in context it closes an explanation of disaster as covenant punishment, against the page's own point; Luke 13 corrected (Jesus was told, not asked, raised the tower himself, and turned the call to repent on everyone); the Reformed and the Arminian and Wesleyan answers each given their best text and their real comfort, with no landing; God's sharp answer to Job acknowledged. Care: 911 added to the helper's next step. Voice: anaphora cut in the this-week intro and the prayer; the Revelation reading ends on weight rather than recap; a comfortable closing line and a duplicated hospice line cut to keep the page under 4,500 words.
